fields.definition: The central document in Steinberg Cubase that holds all the settings and references for a piece of work, saved as a .cpr file. It stores the track arrangement, mixer and routing settings, edits, and automation, while pointing to the media files kept in the project folder.
fields.plain_english: A Cubase project is the file that holds your whole song in Cubase. It remembers your tracks, edits, and mixer settings. It also links to the audio files saved in the project folder. Think of it as a map that keeps every part of your work together.
fields.purpose_function: It ties every track, edit, mix setting, and media reference into one saved, reopenable state, so a whole production can be stored, recalled, and continued exactly where it was left off.
fields.practical_application: A technician opens, saves, and backs up the .cpr file together with its Audio and other project subfolders, and uses Save As or Back up Project to move or archive a session without losing linked media.
common_mistakes: Moving or renaming the .cpr file but leaving its audio files behind, which breaks the links to the media.
Assuming the project file contains the audio itself, when it mainly references external files in the project folder.
Not saving incremental versions, so one corrupted project file loses all recent work.
scenario_contexts: Starting a new song and choosing a project folder location before recording.
Archiving a finished mix by using Back up Project to gather all referenced media.
Reopening a client session weeks later and having every track, edit, and mix setting recalled.

fields.definition: In REAPER, a user-created macro that combines two or more actions from the Action List so they run in sequence when triggered by a single command, shortcut, or menu item.
fields.plain_english: A custom action in REAPER lets you bundle several commands into one. You pick the steps you want, put them in order, and give them a single shortcut. Pressing that shortcut then runs all the steps for you, like a one-tap recipe.
fields.purpose_function: It speeds up repetitive work by letting one keystroke perform a whole chain of steps, cutting manual clicks and keeping multi-step tasks consistent every time.
fields.practical_application: An engineer builds a custom action to, for example, select tracks, toggle their visibility, and zoom, then assigns it a keyboard shortcut or toolbar button for instant reuse.
common_mistakes: Ordering the steps wrong, so the actions run in a sequence that gives an unexpected result.
Forgetting that some actions apply to whatever is focused or selected, so the macro behaves differently depending on context.
Confusing a custom action, which is a fixed sequence, with a cycle action, which steps through actions on repeated presses.
scenario_contexts: Automating a repetitive editing routine that normally takes several menu clicks.
Creating a single shortcut that sets up a preferred track layout and zoom level.
Sharing a reusable macro with collaborators to standardize a studio workflow.

sources: Sound on Sound, 'Automate Anything With Reaper's Custom Actions'

flags: All fields omitted: 'Cycle action' is a real REAPER SWS/S&M extension feature (an action that advances through a defined list of actions on each successive trigger), but it is documented only in third-party extension wikis/sites, not in two or more sources meeting the strict acceptable-source standard (standards body, manufacturer technical documentation, or recognized professional text). Cannot confirm to the required standard.

fields.definition: In Logic Pro, the strip in the upper part of the ruler used to define a section of the project that plays back or records repeatedly. With Cycle mode on, playback loops between the left and right edges of this highlighted region.
fields.plain_english: The cycle area in Logic Pro is a marked strip along the top ruler. It sets a part of your song to play over and over on a loop. You drag its edges to choose where the loop starts and stops, so you can practice or record a section again and again.
fields.purpose_function: It lets you repeat a chosen section hands-free for focused practice, take recording, or fine-tuning edits and mix moves without constantly restarting playback.
fields.practical_application: A technician drags across the ruler to set the cycle area over a chorus, enables Cycle mode, and loops that part to record several takes or audition edits.
common_mistakes: Leaving Cycle mode on by accident, so playback keeps looping when you expect it to continue past the section.
Setting the cycle edges slightly off the bar lines, causing loops that feel out of time.
Confusing the cycle area, a playback loop range, with looping an individual region.
scenario_contexts: Looping a verse to record several vocal takes for comping.
Repeating a short section to dial in an EQ or effect setting.
Practicing a difficult passage by playing it back on a continuous loop.

sources: Apple Logic Pro User Guide, 'Use the cycle area in Logic Pro'
Apple Logic Pro for iPad User Guide, 'Use the cycle area'

The term maps to several unrelated product-specific senses (control-surface editor software, audio-interface control panels, network/monitoring overview screens, and generic status panels) with no established consensus, and no two or more acceptable sources define one canonical audio-technical sense. Flagged pending clarification of the intended sense.

All fields omitted: 'Defeat music' is ambiguous and not attested as a standard term. The closest established concept is the commercial-paging 'music defeat'/priority-mute function (background music muted during an announcement), but this exact phrase and sense are not defined in two or more acceptable manufacturer technical documents, and the intended meaning here is unclear. Flagged pending clarification.

Flagged pending clarification of the intended sense.

fields.definition: A formal confirmation that a finished deliverable has passed quality control and conforms to the recipient's technical delivery specification, covering items such as file format, channel layout, and loudness. It is the sign-off, often documented as a QC report, that clears content for acceptance and distribution.
fields.plain_english: Delivery certification is a formal check that says a finished file meets all the rules the client set. It confirms the format, channels, and loudness are right and that quality control found no faults. Think of it like a pass stamp that lets the file be accepted and released.
fields.purpose_function: It protects both sides by proving, before acceptance, that the master meets the agreed spec, so faulty or non-compliant files are caught before they reach air or release.
fields.practical_application: Before hand-off, an engineer or QC operator checks the deliverable against the spec sheet and provides certification or a QC report confirming it passes.
common_mistakes: Treating certification as a formality and skipping an actual check against the spec sheet.
Judging loudness by ear instead of measuring it to the required target.
Missing required elements, such as channel layout or metadata, that the specification demands.
scenario_contexts: Confirming a broadcast master meets the network's loudness and format spec before hand-off.
Providing a QC pass report with files delivered to a streaming platform.
Rejecting and returning a deliverable that fails the technical specification.

sources: EBU R128 (Loudness normalisation and permitted maximum level of audio signals)
Sound on Sound, 'Mastering Essentials: Final Delivery, Requirements & Specs'

fields.definition: The final approved version of a mix or master prepared to meet the exact technical specifications of its destination, such as a streaming service, broadcaster, or replication plant. It is the file or file set formally handed over for distribution, made to the required format, sample rate, bit depth, and loudness targets.
fields.plain_english: A delivery master is the final, approved version of a track made to fit exactly what the client or platform asks for. It uses the right file type, quality, and loudness for that destination. Think of it as the finished copy you hand over for release, cut to spec.
fields.purpose_function: It exists to give each destination a correctly formatted, compliant file so the release plays back and measures as intended without any further changes.
fields.practical_application: A mastering engineer renders separate delivery masters for streaming, CD, and video, each matching that platform's format and loudness requirements before sending them off.
common_mistakes: Sending one generic file to every platform instead of meeting each one's format and loudness spec.
Over-limiting to a very loud level that gets turned down and can distort under loudness normalization.
Mislabeling sample rate, bit depth, or channel layout so the file is rejected in QC.
scenario_contexts: Preparing separate masters for a streaming service, an online store, and a CD run.
Delivering a broadcast mix that must meet a specified loudness target.
Sending an approved final file set to a distributor or replication plant.

sources: Sound on Sound, 'Mastering Essentials: Final Delivery, Requirements & Specs'
Ballou, Handbook for Sound Engineers (mastering and delivery)
